'''''Melaleuca armillaris''''', commonly known as '''bracelet honey myrtle''', is a plant in the myrtle [[Family (taxonomy)|family]], [[Myrtaceae]], and is native to [[South Australia]], [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]] and [[Tasmania]] in south-eastern [[Australia]]. It is a hardy, commonly grown species, often used as a fast-growing screen plant. It has become naturalised in [[Western Australia]] and parts of Victoria. In its natural state, it grows on coastal cliffs and along estuaries.

==Description==
Bracelet honey myrtle ranges from a large shrub to a small weeping tree growing to {{convert|8|m|ft|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} in height. It has rough, grey fibrous bark, distinctive decumbent branching and dense foliage. The leaves are arranged in alternating pairs ([[Decussation|"decussate"]]) at right angles to the pairs above and below so that they appear to be in four rows along the stem.<ref name=Brophy>{{cite book|last1=Brophy|first1=Joseph J.|last2=Craven|first2=Lyndley A.|last3=Doran|first3=John C.|title=Melaleucas : their botany, essential oils and uses|date=2013|publisher=Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research|page=80|location=Canberra|isbn=9781922137517}}</ref> (One source<ref name=Holliday>{{cite book|last1=Holliday|first1=Ivan|title=Melaleucas : a field and garden guide|date=2004|publisher=Reed New Holland Publishers|location=Frenchs Forest, N.S.W.|isbn=1876334983|pages=24–25|edition=2nd}}</ref> describes the leaves as being spirally arranged and another as being alternate.<ref name=plantnet>{{cite web|title=''Melaleuca armillaris''|url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Melaleuca~armillaris|publisher=Plantnet: Royal Botanic Garden Sydney|accessdate=30 April 2015}}</ref>) The leaves are {{convert|4.5-19|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long, {{convert|0.8-4|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} wide and [[Glabrousness|glabrous]] except when very young, linear to narrow oval in shape, with the end tapering to a distinct hook.<ref name=Brophy/><ref name=Holliday /><ref name=plantnet/>

The flowers are white, sometimes cream-coloured, rarely pink, and are arranged in cylindrical spikes on the sides of branches, often on older wood. The spikes are up to {{convert|50|mm|in|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|25|mm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter and contain a large number of individual flowers. The petals are {{convert|1.5-3|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long and fall off as the flower matures. The stamens are arranged in five bundles known as staminal claws, which are  {{convert|3-4.9|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long with each bundle containing eight to 18 stamens. The flowering season is mostly spring to early summer and is followed by fruit which are woody [[Capsule (botany)|capsules]], {{convert|2.3-4.5|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long and about {{convert|5|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} in diameter, in cylindrical clusters along the branches.<ref name=Brophy/><ref name=Holliday /><ref name=plantnet/>  
[[File:Melaleuca armillaris-Flowers.jpg|thumb|210px|[[Inflorescence]] showing stamen bundles]]

==Taxonomy and naming==
The species was first formally described in 1788 by [[Joseph Gaertner]] in ''[[De Fructibus et Seminibus Plantarum]]''<ref name=Gaertner>{{cite book|last1=Gaertner|first1=Joseph|title=De Fructibus et Seminibus Plantarum|date=1788|volume=1 |page=171|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/114363#page/185/mode/1up|accessdate=30 April 2015}}</ref> from specimens collected by [[Joseph Banks]] during an expedition of [[James Cook]] to Australia. It was then given the name ''Metrosideros armillaris'' by [[Daniel Solander]].<ref name=APNI(1)>{{cite web|title=''Metrosideros armillaris''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/541401|publisher=APNI|accessdate=30 April 2015}}</ref>  The species was renamed ''Melaleuca armillaris'' in 1797 by [[James Edward Smith (botanist)|James Edward Smith]] in ''Transactions of the [[Linnean Society of London]]''.<ref name=APNI(2)>{{cite web|title=''Melaleuca armillaris''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/508941|publisher=APNI|accessdate=30 April 2015}}</ref><ref name=Linnean>{{cite journal|last1=Smith|first1=James Edward|title=Botanical Characters of Some Plants of the Natural Order of Myrti|journal=Transactions of the Linnean Society of London|date=1797|volume=3|page=277|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/13713#page/304/mode/1up|accessdate=30 April 2015}}</ref> The [[Botanical name|specific epithet]] (''armillaris'') is from the [[Latin]] ''armilla'', meaning "a bracelet", apparently in reference to the appearance of the cylinder of fruits on the branches.<ref name="Brophy" />

The two subspecies are:
*''Melaleuca armillaris'' subsp. ''armillaris'' which is the more common and widespread subspecies;<ref name=APNI(3)>{{cite web|title=''Melaleuca armillaris'' subsp. ''armillaris''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/name/apni/118072 |publisher=APNI|accessdate=30 April 2015}}</ref>
*''Melaleuca armillaris.'' subsp. ''akineta'' <small>F.C.Quinn</small><ref name=APNI(4)>{{cite web|title=''Melaleuca armillaris'' subsp. ''akineta''|url=https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/552334|publisher=APNI|accessdate=30 April 2015}}</ref> which has shorter stamens and fewer flowers in the [[inflorescence]].<ref name=Brophy /><ref name=Holliday />

==Distribution and habitat==
Subspecies ''armillaris'' occurs in coastal areas south of the [[Manning River]] district in New South Wales to far eastern Victoria, some of the [[Bass Strait]] islands including [[Curtis Island (Tasmania)|Curtis Island]] and the far north eastern corner of Tasmania. It is also naturalised in other parts of Victoria, the [[Australian Capital Territory]], the south of South Australia and the south-west of Western Australia.<ref name=Brophy/> It is especially common on the far south coast of New South Wales. It grows naturally on coastal headlands and clifftops, often in dense heath. Subspecies ''akineta'' is only found in the [[Gawler Ranges]] of South Australia, where it grows on ridges and granite outcrops.<ref name=Brophy/><ref name=Holliday/>

==Use in horticulture==
''Melaleuca armillaris'' is cultivated as a fast-growing windbreak or screening plant. It is hardy and will grow in most soils and aspects, resistant to salt spray and suitable for growing under power lines.<ref name=Wrigley>{{cite book|last1=Wrigley|first1=John|last2=Fagg|first2=Murray|title=Australian native plants : a manual for their propagation, cultivation and use in landscaping|date=1983|publisher=Collins|location=Sydney|isbn=0002165759|page=261|edition=2nd}}</ref>

==Ecology==
This melaleuca is regarded as a serious environmental weed in some locations especially in Victoria. It replaces local species and increases fuel loads making areas more prone to [[Bushfires in Australia|bushfires]]. After a bushfire, the problem is increased because of the plants' releasing large numbers of seeds after fire. In South Australia, it is a problem in the [[Mount Lofty Ranges]], [[Adelaide Hills]], and [[Kangaroo Island]]. In Western Australia, the problems occur in coastal areas of the south-west of that state.<ref name=Qld>{{cite web|title=Bracelet honey-myrtle|url=http://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/media/Html/melaleuca_armillaris.htm|publisher=Queensland government|accessdate=25 January 2018}}</ref>

Bracelet honey myrtle is a preferred food of species of [[sawfly]] (order [[Hymenoptera]], suborder Symphaptera), especially the long-tailed sawfly ''[[Pterygophorus facielongus]]'', which can rapidly defoliate an entire tree.<ref name=museum>{{cite web|title=Sawflies|url=http://australianmuseum.net.au/sawflies|publisher=Australian Museum|accessdate=30 April 2015}}</ref>

''Melaleuca armillaris'' has the potential to become a weed beyond its native range, and is regarded as a serious environmental weed in Victoria and South Australia, where it has the potential to increase fuel loads and make these areas more prone to fires.<ref name="Weeds">{{cite web |title=''Melaleuca armillaris'' |url=https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/media/Html/melaleuca_armillaris.htm#:~:text=Bracelet%20honey%2Dmyrtle%20(Melaleuca%20armillaris,coastal%20ranges%20in%20eastern%20Australia |publisher=Weeds of Australia |access-date=25 November 2024}}</ref>
